item.title: Genome engineering with base editors: Technological advancements enabling clinical translation.
item.abstract: Base editors (BEs) are precision genome editing tools which allow for the efficient introduction of point mutations in live cells without using double-strand DNA breaks. The two main classes of BEs are cytosine base editors (CBEs) and adenine base editors (ABEs), which can introduce C•G to T•A and A•T to G•C mutations, respectively. Since their development, BEs have been further developed and improved to address issues related to efficiency, specificity, and precision. In this review, we briefly summarize several recent notable developments in the field relevant to their path to the clinic, as well as three clinical trials from the past three years which apply BEs to the treatment of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, hypercholesterolemia, and a rare N = 1 urea cycle disorder. In these examples, base editing is used to precisely knock out genes or correct mutations back to wild-type in blood disorders and liver diseases. Through clinical trials, patients around the world are being treated with BE therapeutics, ushering in the next generation of precision medicine.

item.title: Biomolecular design through latent reasoning with RFD4-Proteina
item.abstract: Biomolecular design requires finding chemically and geometrically compatible arrangements of interacting atoms and molecules. The complexity of problems which can be tackled by deep learning design models is limited by both the molecular landscape they encompass and their ability to explore that landscape effectively. Here we introduce RFD4-Proteina, which addresses these limitations through intrinsic and extrinsic reasoning within a shared chemical and conformational latent space. The latent space encompasses standard and modified amino acids, sugars, DNA, and RNA, with force-field supervision favoring physically plausible atomic reconstructions. Within this space, intrinsic reasoning uses recurrent refinement to adaptively allocate computation, while extrinsic reasoning guides search with arbitrary constraints such as energetic or geometric criteria. Across in silico protein design benchmarks, RFD4-Proteina achieves higher design success rates at greater generation throughput than all previous methods evaluated, with further gains from conformational flexibility, recurrent refinement, and search. The same model performs equivalently to or better than state-of-the-art specialist methods for side-chain packing, sequence design, conformational sampling, and design refinement. We demonstrate the power and versatility of RFD4-Proteina experimentally by designing specific and cross-reactive binders to therapeutically relevant targets, recognizing phosphorylations, controlling glycosylation, and creating enzymes that catalyze both bond-breaking and bond-forming reactions, including a first proof-of-concept demonstration of a de novo designed enzyme for active pharmaceutical ingredient synthesis. By unifying diverse chemistry, conformational flexibility, and scalable reasoning in a single physically grounded latent space, RFD4-Proteina expands the frontier of biomolecular design.

item.title: Microliter to liter scale engineering of cell-free 1,2,4-butanetriol biosynthesis.
item.abstract: Biomanufacturing offers sustainable alternatives to traditional chemical synthesis under milder temperatures and pressures. However, the slow pace and iterative engineering bottlenecks of cell strain development restrict the feasible biological design space. Cell-free systems circumvent these constraints, providing a flexible and high-throughput screening approach to accelerate pathway prototyping and enzyme optimization, yet they are not typically used for manufacturing scale-up. To evaluate the scalability of cell-free biosynthesis, we establish an end-to-end fully cell-free architecture to discover, develop, and scale the biosynthesis of 1,2,4-butanetriol (BT), a high-value industrial platform chemical. First, we systematically screened ∼150 enzymes across the 4-step pathway from xylose to BT to identify highly active homologs for each reaction. Next, we applied statistical Design of Experiments to optimize reaction formulations for cost and titer. Finally, the maximum-titer and minimum-cost formulations were scaled up across five orders of magnitude, from 10 μL to 1 L reactions. This resulted in peak volumetric productivities of ∼1 g/L/h and titers over 13 g of BT in a single 1 L reaction, with reagent costs totaling just $3.00 per liter. This work expands the diversity of enzymes tested for BT synthesis and establishes a blueprint for advancing industrial biochemical manufacturing fully in vitro, opening future opportunities for bioreactor integration with continuous or fed-batch operation and online product recovery.

item.abstract: Driven by deep-learning methods, computational protein design can now rapidly generate de novo structures, opening new frontiers for creating proteins that bind small molecules tightly and specifically, although achieving predictable and tunable binding remains challenging. item.title: Reprogramming Protein Function by Expanding Chemical and Combinatorial Space: Integrating Chemical and Computational Strategies.
item.abstract: Proteins are biological macromolecules that perform critical functions, including catalysis, molecular recognition, and cellular regulation. Natural evolution has generated remarkable protein diversity, leaving vast opportunities for engineered molecular innovation. Protein engineering has evolved from the rational design of proteins over the last few decades to approaches based on directed evolution and computational methods to enhance their properties. Protein engineering is shifting from optimization-based approaches to an integrated approach, which includes rational design, directed evolution, computational and generative modeling, synthetic chemistry, synthetic biology, and laboratory automation. These strategies widen the scope of experimentally accessible chemical and structural toolboxes in proteins without sacrificing the physicochemical constraints, cellular compatibility, evolutionary processes, and experimental validation. Meanwhile, synthetic chemistry is extending the natural abilities of proteins by incorporating noncanonical amino acids, novel cofactors, and modified metal centers and catalytic environments. These technologies enable the creation of artificial enzymes, programmed molecular binders, synthetic receptors, molecular machines, and biomaterials that have functions beyond those of their natural counterparts. This review introduces advances in the protein engineering field, from past methods of modifying proteins to present-day opportunities for generating proteins with artificial intelligence, and explains how the fields of computation, chemistry, and biology are driving the future of programmable proteins.

item.title: An endogenous-signal-guided growth-coupled selection platform for glycosyltransferase evolution in Escherichia coli K5.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Directed evolution of polysaccharide glycosyltransferases remains constrained by the absence of scalable selection outputs that report pathway-relevant enzyme function in living cells. Here, we developed an endogenous-signal-guided growth-coupled selection platform for glycosyltransferase evolution in Escherichia coli K5, a bacterium that naturally produces heparosan.
RESULTS: By comparing a heparosan-deficient kfiA-deletion chassis with the parental strain, we prioritized the promoter upstream of ECK5_RS12660 (designated Pgnt) as a production-state-associated regulatory element. CRP was nominated as a functional amplifier of Pgnt output using DNA pull-down, proteomic prioritization, and inducible transcription-factor screening. To convert this endogenous regulatory response into a practical selection interface, we constructed a clean K5AC chassis lacking kfiA and kfiC, and benchmarked Pgnt-only and CRP-assisted circuits against NaKfiA variants across a defined activity gradient. Pgnt alone showed weak and non-monotonic reporter behavior, whereas CRP assistance generated a dual fluorescence/growth output that supported tetracycline-coupled enrichment of the highest-ranking benchmark variant. Targeted PmHS2 library selection further recovered recurrent substitutions, and reconstruction-based biochemical validation confirmed five activity-enhancing variants. Whole-genome diversification revealed a boundary condition for this selection logic, as the recovered K5-WGE strain did not show increased final heparosan production under the tested conditions. Analysis of endogenous kfiA/kfiC variants further showed that growth-coupled output can reflect complex-associated glycosyltransferase states rather than isolated KfiA catalytic activity alone. Because CRP was supplied from the same pBAD-controlled module in all benchmark and library comparisons, fluorescence and tetracycline-growth outputs were interpreted as circuit-level enrichment signals within a fixed assay configuration; productive mutations were assigned only after reconstruction and orthogonal biochemical validation.
CONCLUSIONS: The Pgnt-CRP module provides an endogenous-signal-guided enrichment interface for targeted glycosyltransferase libraries. Its fluorescence and growth outputs integrate promoter activity, fixed CRP amplification, and host physiology; reconstruction and orthogonal biochemical validation are required to assign productive enzyme improvement.

item.title: Enzymatic strategies for PET valorization: Advances in discovery, engineering, and cyanobacterial chassis development.
item.abstract: The global accumulation of plastic waste has intensified the need for sustainable technologies capable of replacing conventional mechanical and chemical recycling. During the past decade, enzymatic plastic biodegradation has rapidly evolved from the identification of individual depolymerases to an interdisciplinary research field integrating environmental microbiology, artificial intelligence, protein engineering, systems biology, and synthetic biology. Despite remarkable progress, current research remains largely fragmented, with enzyme discovery, catalytic optimization, and downstream plastic valorization often being developed independently, thereby limiting the establishment of integrated plastic biomanufacturing platforms. In this review, we critically synthesize advances in plastic-degrading enzymes, covering meta-omics and AI-assisted enzyme discovery, protein engineering strategies that improve catalytic efficiency, thermostability, and substrate specificity, and metabolic engineering approaches for assimilating plastic-derived monomers into value-added products. Rather than viewing these advances as separate research directions, we propose an integrated biotechnology framework that connects environmental enzyme mining, AI-driven protein engineering, microbial metabolic rewiring, and photosynthetic cell factories into a unified plastic-to-product strategy. Recent progress in heterologous protein secretion and metabolic engineering in cyanobacteria supports the continued exploration of solar-powered microbial platforms; however, complete PET-to-product bioconversion in cyanobacteria remains conceptual and has not yet been experimentally demonstrated. We anticipate that the convergence of multi-omics, artificial intelligence, enzyme engineering, and synthetic biology will shift the field from improving individual plastic-degrading enzymes toward constructing complete microbial plastic bioconversion systems, thereby accelerating the realization of a sustainable circular plastic bioeconomy.

item.title: Targeted design of next-generation electroactive microorganisms.
item.abstract: Bioelectrochemical systems (BESs) convert chemical energy into electrical energy or vice versa by utilizing microorganisms. Early proof-of-concept studies employed wild-type electroactive microorganisms (EAMs) that can exchange electrons with external acceptors such as electrodes, a process called extracellular electron transfer (EET). However, wild-type EAMs are limited by modest performance, restricted product spectra, and complex process control. A deeper understanding of the molecular EET mechanisms has allowed a targeted enhancement of BES processes. Advances in genetic and metabolic engineering have enabled increased electron transfer rates, redox pathway rewiring, and broader product spectra, expanding the potential of BESs by generating engineered, next-generation EAMs (ngEAMs). This review outlines recent advances and strategies for target identification and for process-tailored, ngEAMs, and their application in processes of high interest to biotechnology.

item.title: CRISPR-Cas Systems in Protozoan Parasites: Genome Editing, Functional Genomics, Gene Regulation and Emerging Applications.
item.abstract: Protozoan parasites possess complex genomes, unusual DNA-repair mechanisms, multiple developmental stages, and, in several species, intracellular or vector-dependent life cycles that complicate functional genetic studies. CRISPR-Cas9 has become a central tool for functional genomics in these organisms, enabling targeted gene disruption, replacement, tagging, nucleotide modification and genome-wide functional screening. However, editing efficiency and outcomes vary substantially among parasite species and depend not only on Cas9-mediated double-strand break formation but also on target accessibility, guide design, delivery method, parasite stage, DNA-repair capacity, donor availability, selection and the biological cost of the induced lesion. This review focuses primarily on experimentally established Cas9-mediated genome editing in Plasmodium, Leishmania, Toxoplasma gondii, Trypanosoma, Babesia, Theileria and Cryptosporidium. We compare plasmid-based and transient expression, ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, electroporation/nucleofection, stage-specific delivery, guide and donor design, selection strategies, editing outcomes, and molecular and functional validation. Particular emphasis is placed on homology-directed repair (HDR), canonical non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ) and single-strand annealing (SSA), which determine whether editing results in indels, precise sequence replacement, tagging or larger genomic deletions. Species-specific differences are illustrated by efficient NHEJ-mediated disruption in Toxoplasma, donor-dependent repair in Plasmodium and Cryptosporidium, SSA-associated repair in Leishmania, efficient homologous recombination in trypanosomatids, precise editing in Babesia, and stage-specific delivery constraints in Theileria. The review further examines the progression from single-gene editing to marker-free manipulation, base editing, conditional approaches and genome-wide functional screens. Cas12a, CRISPRi/a, prime editing and related systems are discussed as emerging extensions. Overall, this repair- and delivery-centred framework explains why CRISPR editing differs among protozoan parasites and identifies the experimentally validated limitations that currently shape their genome-engineering potential.

item.title: Prime-LS: a cryoprotectant-free, lyophilized MSC-secretome conferring protection against acute experimental colitis in vivo.
item.abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic, immune-mediated disorder characterized by recurrent mucosal inflammation and epithelial damage. Its incidence is rising, while current therapies fail to achieve durable remission due to limited efficacy or adverse effects. Cell-free approaches based on the mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) secretome offer an alternative with improved safety and scalability. In this study, we present Prime-LS, an excipient-free, off-the-shelf MSC-secretome biologic that retains immunomodulatory activity without cryoprotectants. In vitro, Prime-LS suppressed proliferation of peripheral blood mononuclear cells, while in vivo subcutaneous dosing in a murine colitis model prevented disease onset, preserved mucosal integrity, and normalized inflammation. Together, these findings support Prime-LS as a stable, functionally preserved MSC-secretome formulation with potential for further translational development in UC and other immune-mediated diseases.

item.title: Engineered IGF-I-loaded extracellular vesicles restore hepatic regeneration capacity after partial hepatectomy in fibrotic livers.
item.abstract: Liver regeneration following surgical resection is frequently compromised in clinically relevant settings, including extended hepatectomy, increasing the risk of post-hepatectomy liver failure. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are emerging as a cell-free therapeutic platform with regenerative and immunomodulatory activity through delivery of bioactive cargo. Here, we evaluated EVs derived from human umbilical cord perivascular cells (HUCPVCs), an MSC population engineered to express insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-I), in partial hepatectomy models in healthy and fibrotic livers in mice. Administration of IGF-I-EVs reduced early liver injury and significantly enhanced liver mass recovery and hepatocyte proliferation. Mechanistically, IGF-I-EVs activated core regenerative gene programs in whole-liver tissue and in isolated hepatocytes. In parallel, IGF-I-EV treatment reprogrammed hepatic macrophages toward a pro-resolutive/regenerative phenotype, characterized by IGF-I receptor signaling activation and induction of hepatotrophic factors. IGF-I-EVs also directly modulated hepatic stellate cells, reducing fibrogenic marker expression and inducing Hgf, through both direct EV action and indirect effects mediated by the macrophage secretome. Notably, IGF-I-EVs partially restored regenerative competence in established fibrosis and promoted remodeling of the fibrotic architecture. Together, these findings support IGF-I-engineered MSC-derived EVs as a cell-free strategy to enhance liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy in settings of impaired regenerative capacity.

item.title: What's Hot and What's New in Xenotransplantation From the Young Investigator Committee of the IXA-Clinical Science.
item.abstract: The 2025 International Xenotransplantation Association (IXA) Congress in Geneva, convened in parallel with World Health Organization meetings on xenotransplantation guidance, marked a transition in clinical xenotransplantation from demonstrating that pig organs can function in humans to defining how graft injury is detected, interpreted, and managed in real time. We synthesize the major clinical themes that emerged from the meeting across kidney, heart, liver, and lung xenotransplantation. In kidney xenotransplantation, the NYU and Massachusetts General Hospital living-recipient experiences now delineate two complementary injury patterns-antibody- and complement-driven with a membranoproliferative, IgA-positive, innate-rich phenotype, and T cell-mediated with persistent innate immune activation-both converging on macrophage and NK-cell biology that conventional immunosuppression does not address. The first registration-supporting Phase 1/2/3 trial of a 10-gene-edited xenokidney (EXPAND) has begun, framed by IXA position-paper recommendations and supported by recent FDA approvals. In cardiac xenotransplantation, real-time complement-function monitoring, global longitudinal strain, and donor-derived cell-free DNA emerge as an actionable surveillance toolkit, while other allotransplant biomarkers translate poorly. In liver xenotransplantation, extracorporeal cross-circulation and the first preliminary data describing auxiliary pig-to-human liver transplant (171-day survival) position porcine livers as bridge-support platforms rather than definitive replacements. Lung xenotransplantation remains confined to ex vivo perfusion and short-term preclinical models. Cross-cutting priorities include donor-pig design and individual graft phenotyping that accounts for transgene expression heterogeneity, prospectively validated multimodal monitoring, management of nephrotic-range proteinuria and associated urinary loss of biologic immunosuppressants, and dedicated registry, ethical, and patient-engagement infrastructure to support trustworthy clinical expansion.

item.title: Multimodal Biomarkers in Pancreatic Cancer: From Early Detection to Precision Therapy.
item.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains highly lethal, with a 5-year relative survival of ∼13%. For decades, CA19-9 has been the principal clinical biomarker, but its limitations-including nonsecretion in Lewis-negative individuals, false-positive elevations with cholestasis, and inadequate sensitivity for early detection-have driven a rapidly expanding biomarker landscape. Blood-based multianalyte assays integrating circulating proteins, glycoproteins, methylated cell-free DNA, and tumor-derived signals, together with imaging-based deep learning, are improving early detection beyond CA19-9 alone. Molecular subtyping and postoperative circulating tumor DNA further refine prognosis, while germline and somatic alterations-including BRCA1/2/PALB2, MSI-H/dMMR, NRG1 fusions, KRAS G12C, NTRK, FGFR2, and BRAF V600E-are increasingly enabling biomarker-directed therapy. The next frontier is prospective validation and clinical integration of multimodal biomarkers to enable earlier diagnosis, more precise risk stratification, and equitable delivery of precision therapy.

item.title: Recent advances in fabrication strategies, functional modulation and healthcare applications of native protein-based hydrogels.
item.abstract: Native protein-based hydrogels not only possess all advantages of their denatured analogues such as exceptional biocompatibility and low toxicity, but also retain the intrinsic function of the protein building block. Therefore, they exhibit novel favorable properties including inherent bioactivity and reversible sol-gel transformation behavior. As such, they have emerged as versatile biomaterials widely used in the biomedical field. This review provides a comprehensive and up-to date overview of design strategies, formation mechanisms, and healthcare applications of native protein-based hydrogels. We systematically summarize the key cross-linking strategies for fabricating reversible native protein-based hydrogels, with particular emphasis on how these interactions govern hydrogel formation and their functionality. We highlight recent advances in fabricating these hydrogels through chemical cross-linking, physical cross-linking, metal coordination, fusion protein design, key interface redesign, de novo design, and modular design strategies, which enable precise control over hierarchical architecture, stimuli-responsiveness, and biomechanical properties. Furthermore, we explore the diverse healthcare applications of these hydrogels, with emphasis on drug delivery, wound healing, and tissue engineering. Finally, we discuss perspectives on future directions, including the integration of computational modeling, machine learning, and high-throughput experimentation to enable rational design of smart, multifunctional native protein-based hydrogels with tailored performances for next-generation biomedical applications.

item.title: Galectin-3 links microglial neuroinflammation to Aβ aggregation and lysosomal processing.
item.abstract: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the molecular mechanisms linking microglial dysfunction to amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify galectin-3 (Gal3) as a regulator of plaque-associated microglial responses, linking Aβ aggregation, lysosomal function, and neuritic pathology. Using postmortem brain tissue from AD patients, we found that Gal3+ microglia preferentially associate with cored plaques and correlate with increased LAMP1+ dystrophic neurites. Gal3 was also detected in microglial lysosomal compartments, extramicroglial dystrophic structures, and in association with extracellular amyloid fibrils, suggesting roles in both intracellular and extracellular Aβ processing. In APP mice, Gal3 deficiency reduced plaque burden and neuritic dystrophy, increased plaque compaction, and enhanced TREM2 coverage around amyloid plaques. Mechanistically, in vitro microglial experiments showed that Gal3 modulates Aβ uptake and lysosomal processing, whereas lysosomal dysfunction promoted the accumulation of fibrillar Aβ from initially monomeric species, particularly in Gal3-deficient cells. Cell-free assays demonstrated that Gal3 preferentially binds fibrillar Aβ, inhibits secondary nucleation, and alters fibril morphology, while Gal3-modified fibrillar Aβ reduces N2a neuronal cell number. Finally, in silico structural analyses identified candidate Gal3 interactors enriched in leucine-rich-repeat and immunoglobulin-like proteins, supporting a role for this lectin in immune receptor regulation. Complementary in vivo transcriptomic profiling showed that Gal3 deletion suppresses type I interferon and microglial neurodegenerative transcriptional signatures. Together, these findings position Gal3 at the interface between Aβ remodeling, lysosomal homeostasis, and plaque-associated microglial responses in AD.
